To me it's a case of simple logic and math.

Lets make up an arbitrary measurement of "Pollutions". What pollutions are, exactly, isn't important for the example, but it is important to say that "Pollutions" are responsible for the change in Earths climate.

Lets say man is responsible for 50 pollutions a year.

Lets say a volcano eruption is responsible for 200 pollutions a year.

Clearly mother nature and her Volcano is responsible for more pollutions then man, and since pollutions are what cause the climate to change, it's mother nature that changes the climate and not man right?

Well, not necessarily, because the reality is that it's not a "one or the other" system. Nature doesn't just choose the largest value of pollutions and use it... climate is an effect of the total sum of all pollutions created in a year.

So since man is worth 50, and a volcano is worth 200, the total sum of pollutions generated a years is 250. And last time I checked, 250 > 200. Here we can see that man does indeed have an effect, no matter how small, on the climate of the planet.

Now, you could still argue that the vast majority of the pollutions came from nature, and you wouldn't be wrong (at least in this example)... but you're still willingly ignoring the fact that man did have an impact on the amount of pollutions generated in a year.

If the climate where to change at every... 10,000 pollutions... it would take 50 years for a Volcano to cause a change (10,000 / 200 == 50). But with man... it only takes 40 years to cause a change (10,000 / 250 == 40). Here we can see that although man is responsible for only a small amount of pollutions a year, over a period of time, mans effect actually caused a change in climate 10 years earlier then mother nature had scheduled.

But with Earth, maybe mans effect is minimal. Like maybe its 10 years out of a 10,000,000 year cycle. Or maybe it's even smaller then that. Maybe our value is closer to say, 2 years out of a 10,000,000 year cycle. We're having such a small impact why should we even care right? True... but you still have to, at this time, admit that man did have an impact.

But man, being intelligent, can actively work to change how many pollutions it puts out a year. So with some effort, we could cut our 50 pollutions a year value down to say, 40. It's not much of a change, but it is a change. That would delay the climate change by an entire year (10,000 / 240 == 41). Man is still responsible for bringing on the change in climate early (in 41 years as opposed to mother natures 50), but now we're only 9 years ahead of schedule instead of 10.

And if man worked really, really hard... maybe we could cut our pollutions in half... at which point we only bring on the climate change 6 years early (10,000 / 225 == 44).

And maybe with some real genius thinking, we can actually create a neutral or possibly even a negative impact. If we produced zero pollutions a year, the climate change would happen in 50 years per mother natures plan... and if we were actually good for the environment, and had a pollutions value of -10 (somehow), we could delay the natural climate change by 2 years (10,000 / 190 == 52).

The point is that no matter what our value of "pollutions" is, big or small (unless we're 100% neutral)... there's just no getting around the simple fact that man does indeed have an impact on the climate. How much impact is what's debatable. But to deny it all together is a fools act.
